races.note: Incumbent Josh Green (D) vs. Gary Cordery (R). No U.S. Senate race in 2026. Rated Solid/Safe D by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato.
Ranked-choice voting for Honolulu mayor, city council and prosecuting attorney in a single November election, from 2032, if the Legislature also approves. Yes = adopt RCV.

assessment.threshold: Majority of voters voting on the question. Blank votes don’t count, unlike Hawaii constitutional amendments
assessment.summary: Slightly more likely to pass than fail. Honolulu voters approve most charter amendments, blank ballots don’t count against it, and the Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters and the Star-Advertiser editorial board all back it in a deeply Democratic electorate. The risk is that the Hawaii GOP is campaigning against it, giving it a partisan edge. RCV has also lost recently in large blue electorates (Oregon 42% in 2024). And this is one of 20 charter questions, where tired voters tend to default to No on anything confusing.
for: Supported by the Democratic Party of Hawaiʻi and the League of Women Voters of Hawaiʻi
The Star-Advertiser editorial board recommends Yes
Blank votes are excluded, so the many voters who skip down-ballot charter questions don’t count as No
Delayed to 2032 and contingent on the Legislature, which softens the ‘too fast, too costly’ argument
Hawaii already uses ranked ballots in some special federal and county elections
against: The Hawaii Republican Party (Chair Shirlene Ostrov, Rep. Elijah Pierick) is actively opposing it, and a Star-Advertiser op-ed called RCV something that ‘ruins elections’
It eliminates the familiar primary-plus-general format for city offices
Voters face 20 charter questions, and ballot fatigue pushes undecided voters toward No
RCV measures in large electorates have underperformed partisanship (Oregon 2024: 42%, Colorado 2024: 46.5%)
assessment.finance: Local reporting shows no ballot-issue committee spending for or against Question 5. Ballot-issue committees file with the Hawaii Campaign Spending Commission. Advocacy appears limited to groups like FairVote, LWV and Rank the Vote on the Yes side and the state GOP on the No side.
